blocks.text: Do Smart Systems Emerge on Their Own? Bottom-up Intelligence Taught by Steven Johnson's "Emergence"
Have you ever heard the word "Emergence"?

Steven Johnson's book, "Emergence: The Connected Lives of Ants, Brains, Cities, and Software," is an intellectually stimulating volume that connects these seemingly disparate phenomena with a single thread.
Today, while unraveling the contents of this book, I would like to consider a certain doubt that those of us who launch new services or projects tend to harbor.
That doubt is: Does the concept of self-organization simply become an excuse for an unplanned way of working?
The Shock of Brainless Organisms
At the beginning of this book, a very impressive organism appears.
It is the slime mold.
This organism lives separately as single-celled amoebas under normal conditions.
However, when the environment deteriorates, they aggregate in units of tens of thousands and begin to move as if they were one giant organism.
Why can they gather and move as if they had arranged it, despite having no brain or nervous system?
There is no leader here.
This is the core theme of the book: Bottom-up Intelligence.
It is a phenomenon where high-level intelligence, which did not exist before, surfaces through the gathering of simple individuals at the lower level, rather than through orders from above.
The author calls this "Emergence."
The Myth of the Ant Queen
When we look at organizations or systems, we unintentionally look for "who is giving the instructions."
The author named this "The Myth of the Ant Queen."
It is a selfish human assumption that because the ant colony is so brilliantly controlled, the queen ant must be giving orders to all the worker ants.
In reality, the queen ant is nothing more than an egg-laying machine.
Smart systems in nature are created entirely from the bottom up, not top-down.
So, why is order maintained even though there is no command tower?
Three Keys to Creating Emergence
The author lists several important keywords as mechanisms for emergence to occur.
The first is Neighbor Interaction.
Ants do not overlook the entire colony.
They only see the fellows right next to them or the pheromones at their feet.
The basic rule is to exchange information only with local neighbors, not the entire system.
The second is Feedback Loops.
There are two types of this.
Positive feedback, where an action accelerates the next action, and negative feedback, which suppresses excess.
By balancing these two, the system adapts without going out of control or stagnating.
The third is Pattern Recognition.
Even if individual elements understand nothing, the system as a whole senses specific trends or shapes.
It is the same logic as our brain recognizing "this is an apple" as a whole, even though a single neuron understands nothing.
Is It an Excuse for Unplanned "Cowboys"?
Now, this is where we apply this to our work.
No leader, individuals moving as they please.
At first glance, this might sound like an affirmation of a chaotic state, often called "Cowboy Coding" in the software development world.
Cowboy coding refers to a state where members write programs as they please, relying only on their own wits without discipline, much like cowboys in a Western movie.
In a business context, it would be a state of pushing forward with individual ideas without plans or manuals.
However, Johnson's answer is NO.
Emergence and disorder are completely different.
Disorderly projects have no rules.
On the other hand, emergent systems have strict rules.
Borrowing the words of urban theorist Jane Jacobs, the author described this as a "Street Ballet."
On the sidewalks of a vibrant city, people pass each other as if dancing a complex dance in silence, monitoring each other, and maintaining order and safety.
This works not because they are walking as they please, but because they are following shared local rules such as distance from others and manners.
Service Developers Become Gardeners
What happens if you are creating a new service and continue to implement fragments of interesting features without deciding too much on the overall picture?
If those fragments do not interact with each other, it is just a jumble of miscellaneous functions.
However, if you carefully design the fragments to cause neighbor interaction, fun and convenience beyond the developer's imagination will be born there.
Johnson calls this an Emergent Property.
It is a magical characteristic that does not exist in individual parts but appears for the first time when they become a whole.
It is the same as how individual water molecules do not have the property of being "wet," but when they gather, the property of water appears.
In this way, a system that changes itself according to the environment and creates unexpected order is called an Adaptive Complex System.

If we aim for the development of emergent services, we need to have the perspective of a Gardener who sows seeds, prepares the environment, and watches over the plants as they grow, rather than an Architect who manages every movement.
Conclusion
Steven Johnson's "Emergence" is not an optimistic book that says "it will get better on its own if left alone."
It is an explanation of the precise mechanism of "how simple rules create complex intelligence."
Reading this book should reveal the borderline of where to control and where to let free in your project management or team building.
